ch03.note: A chaibaidang: one of the swindlers of old Shanghai who courted a woman under false pretenses to strip her of her money. The list here runs from the petty street ruffian up to this practiced confidence-man.

Like the other streets of the French Concession, this one bore a French name; it is Changle Road today. Throughout the chapter the author gives such present-day names in parentheses, a help to the modern Shanghai reader.

A comprador (maiban) was the Chinese manager who handled a foreign firm's dealings with the local market. The title carried an air of wealth and Western connection, which is why the caller offers it as a credential.

ch03.anchor: member of the Standing Committee of the Party's Central Politburo
ch03.note: Luo Yinong (1902–1928) rose through the Shanghai workers' movement to the Party's top councils. His arrest and execution in April 1928, the subject of this chapter, are recorded across the Party's own accounts; the shooting at Longhua is usually dated 21 April 1928.

ch03.anchor: Communist University of the Toilers of the East in Moscow
ch03.note: Known by its Russian initials KUTV, this Comintern school in Moscow trained revolutionaries from across Asia; a great part of the early Chinese Communist leadership passed through it.

ch03.anchor: speaking at a forum marking the hundredth
ch03.note: Hu Jintao was then General Secretary of the Communist Party and, from 2003, President of China (in office to 2012–13). Such centenary tributes are the Party's formal way of fixing a figure's place in its own history.

Zheng Chaolin (1901–1998), editor of Bolshevik and later a leading Chinese Trotskyist, spent decades in Nationalist and then Communist prisons. His detailed memoirs are among the fullest first-hand sources for the underground of these years, and the author leans on them heavily, discrepancies and all.

Xiang xiu, the silk embroidery of Hunan, is counted one of China's four great embroidery traditions; Changsha is its center. That so much of it hung on the walls is the author's quiet mark of a household living beyond an underground worker's means.

ch03.anchor: the large pearls and the small came pattering onto the jade plate
ch03.note: An echo of Bai Juyi's Song of the Pipa (9th century), whose famous line likens the notes of the lute to large and small pearls falling on a plate of jade. Li Zheshi is remembering how easily Qu Qiubai, unlike her husband, could make music.

ch03.anchor: you cut it and it will not part, you smooth it and it snarls again
ch03.note: From a lyric by Li Yu (937–978), the last ruler of the Southern Tang, on the tangle of parting sorrow; the next phrase Li Zheshi quotes, “a taste all its own upon the heart,” is from the same poem.
Panghuang (1926), the second collection of short stories by Lu Xun (1881–1936), modern China's foremost writer. The Beixin Book Company was a well-known Shanghai literary press.
The wave of arrests and executions the Kuomintang loosed on the Communists from April 1927, which drove the Party underground and forms the backdrop to this whole book.

Chen Yannian (1898–1927), eldest son of the Party's founder Chen Duxiu and secretary of its Jiangsu committee, was captured and killed in Shanghai in the summer of 1927. His younger brother Chen Qiaonian, named earlier at the wedding, was killed the following year.

ch03.anchor: Xia Minghan, and others were killed
ch03.note: Xia Minghan (1900–1928), a Hunan Communist, was executed at Wuhan in March 1928, leaving the much-quoted lines “kill me, no matter—there are those who come after.” The source prints his given name with a variant character (the martyr's name is standardly written 夏明翰).
Bolshevik (Bu'ersaiweike) was the Party Center's chief theoretical journal from 1927 to 1932, edited in this very house.
The vast walled estate (Aili Garden) of Silas Aaron Hardoon, a Baghdadi-Jewish magnate who became one of Shanghai's richest men; it was a landmark of the western Settlement.

ch03.anchor: a hotel near the Great World
ch03.note: The Great World (Da Shijie), a many-storied amusement arcade opened in 1917, was among the most famous pleasure resorts of Shanghai and a useful crowd to disappear into.

Deng Xiaoping (1904–1997), then a young secretary at the Party Center and here an eyewitness to Luo Yinong's arrest, would half a century later become China's paramount leader. His daughter's memoir, cited below as Maomao, is the source for his account.

ch03.anchor: men of the Green and Red Gangs
ch03.note: The two great Shanghai secret societies. The Green Gang (see the note at Chapter Two) controlled the concession underworld; both were courted, and feared, by every side. Working through them to reach the authorities was standard practice.

Longhua, on Shanghai's southern edge, held the headquarters of the Songhu (Shanghai–Woosung) Garrison and its execution ground, where many Communists were shot in these years. A Chinese prisoner handed over from the foreign concession would be taken there.

ch03.anchor: Qian Dajun, Commander of the Songhu Garrison
ch03.note: Qian Dajun (1893–1982), a senior Kuomintang general close to Chiang Kai-shek, commanded the Shanghai garrison that carried out the execution.
The two crosses stand in the source itself, which reproduces the notice with the words after Chiang's name struck out; nothing has been supplied here.

ch03.anchor: the concubine Comrade Zhu De took
ch03.note: Zhu De (1886–1976), a former Yunnan officer who joined the Party in Germany in 1922 and later became commander-in-chief of the Red Army and the PLA. That He Zhihua was his wife (the scholarship writes her name He Zhihua, 贺治华) and bore him a daughter is well attested; it is the fact that turns this chapter's traitor into a figure out of the Party's own founding household.
Zhu Min (1926–2009), Zhu De's only surviving child, was raised apart from both parents and reared largely by her grandmother; her memoir is the source for the family scenes quoted here.
Zhang Zuolin (1875–1928), the Fengtian warlord who then controlled Beijing and hunted Communists ferociously; to be taken for his agent was a grave suspicion.
A principal road of the International Settlement running west past Jing'an (“Bubbling Well”) Temple; it is Nanjing West Road today.

One of the conflicting later accounts puts a young Kang Sheng (1898–1975) at the head of the killing party. Kang, then a Shanghai underground cadre, would rise to run the Party's security apparatus and become one of the most feared figures of the Cultural Revolution; the attribution is uncorroborated and the author reports it only as one version.

A popular 2009 Chinese television drama (Renjian Zhengdao Shi Cangsang) whose fictional hero Liqing is loosely modeled on figures of the underground war. The author cites it to show how the episode has passed into legend, not as evidence.
The Huishen Gongxie, the tribunal of mixed foreign and Chinese jurisdiction that handled cases arising in the concessions.

The learned old prisoner of Alexandre Dumas's The Count of Monte Cristo, who teaches the hero to find a crime's author by asking who profits from it—the ancient maxim cui bono. The author borrows it to reopen the question of He Zhihua's motive.

ch03.anchor: recruited Yang Dengying (also called Bao Junfu)
ch03.note: Yang Dengying, under the cover name Bao Junfu, became the Party's first double agent planted inside the enemy's own intelligence service—the coup that opens the next chapter.

ch03.anchor: The "Zhihua" of Zhu De's letter is He Zhihua
ch03.note: The narration writes her name He Zhihua with the character 稚; Zhu De's letter, and most of the scholarship, write it with 治. The two are homophones (both romanize Zhihua) and denote the same woman; the discrepancy is the source's, left as printed.

That He Zhihua survived the 1928 attack, fled, and was later killed is agreed; the manner and date are not. The book places her death at Kaijiang in 1938; other accounts give different years and circumstances. The disagreement is noted here and left unresolved, as the author himself leaves it.
